subject: Tokenizer pathologies and subword fertility as a limiting factor in low-resource multilingual fine-tuning

Topic: Tokenizer pathologies and subword fertility as a limiting factor in low-resource multilingual fine-tuning

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-220)
response:
When you fine-tune a multilingual model on a low-resource language, the tokenizer was almost certainly built from a corpus dominated by high-resource languages — so the model's vocabulary carves up text in ways optimized for English, Mandarin, or Spanish, not Yoruba or Sindhi. Subword fertility is the ratio of tokens to words for a given language: English might average 1.1–1.3 tokens per word, while an agglutinative or morphologically rich language processed by that same tokenizer might yield 4–8, meaning the model must attend over far more tokens to encode the same semantic content. The central question is whether the representational budget you get per training example — measured in tokens, attention span, and gradient signal — is structurally impaired for your target language before you've written a single line of fine-tuning code.

What a beginner misses is that high fertility doesn't just slow things down; it compounds scarcity. A low-resource language has few training examples to begin with, and each example now encodes less information per token, forces the model to learn longer-range dependencies to recover morphological structure that other languages get "for free" in a single token, and hits sequence length limits sooner — truncating data or forcing shorter context windows. The expert also worries about fertility asymmetry across the training distribution: if your fine-tuning mix is 90% high-resource and 10% low-resource, the optimizer is implicitly incentivized to allocate representation capacity toward the token patterns it sees most, further marginalizing the already-sparse subwords of the target language.

prompt:
If you could only intervene at one point — tokenizer design, vocabulary extension, or fine-tuning data weighting — which would have the highest leverage, and what evidence would you need to justify that choice over the others?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-221)
response:
Vocabulary extension has the highest leverage because it attacks the root cause — fertility — without requiring you to retrain from scratch or accept the distortions that pure data weighting introduces. The evidence comes from work like LAPT (Language-Adaptive Pre-Training) and, more directly, Pfeiffer et al. (2021) on MAD-X, where adding target-language tokens to the embedding layer and running masked language modeling on unlabeled target-language text before task fine-tuning produced consistent downstream gains across low-resource African and Asian languages — in some cases 10–20 F1 points on NER — compared to direct fine-tuning on the base multilingual model. Chung et al.'s work on vocabulary extension for mBERT showed that even adding a few hundred carefully chosen subwords for a target language could cut fertility by 30–50% and reduce the token budget required to represent a sentence, giving the fine-tuning signal more semantic density per gradient step. The evidence you'd need to justify this choice over the others: (1) fertility measurements before and after extension showing meaningful reduction, (2) downstream task performance with matched compute budgets across all three intervention types, and (3) crucially, an ablation showing the gain survives when unlabeled target-language data for the extension step is itself scarce — because if it doesn't, you've just pushed the data scarcity problem one level up. Data weighting is the weakest lever alone because it can't compensate for a tokenizer that literally cannot represent the target language's morphology compactly; tokenizer redesign from scratch is highest theoretical leverage but impractical because you lose the pretrained weights entirely unless you do expensive re-initialization work like WECHSEL (Minixhofer et al., 2022), which attempts to transfer embeddings via multilingual word vectors but adds its own fragility.

subject: Tokenizer pathologies and subword fertility as a limiting factor in low-resource multilingual fine-tuning
prompt:
When you extend the vocabulary and initialize the new token embeddings, the initialization strategy is a subtle but high-stakes decision — what are the failure modes of random initialization versus embedding-space interpolation, and under what data conditions does each become dangerous?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-222)
response:
Random initialization of new token embeddings places them at arbitrary positions in an embedding space that has been carefully structured by pretraining — the danger is that the new embeddings start far from any semantically coherent neighborhood, so early fine-tuning gradient steps are essentially wasted rotating them into position rather than learning task-relevant distinctions, and with limited target-language data you may exhaust your fine-tuning budget before they converge to useful representations. Empirically this shows up as unstable training loss curves and, more insidiously, as the model learning to avoid the new tokens by routing predictions through familiar high-resource subword sequences — effectively undoing your vocabulary extension without any explicit signal that this is happening. Embedding-space interpolation — initializing new token embeddings as weighted combinations of the existing subword embeddings that would have tokenized that surface form under the original vocabulary — is the standard mitigation (used in WECHSEL and variants), but its failure mode is semantic averaging artifacts: if the target-language morpheme has no clean compositional relationship to the source subwords, the interpolated initialization can anchor the new embedding in a misleading neighborhood, and the model may converge to a locally consistent but globally wrong representation that's harder to escape than random noise because the gradient signal is small and coherent in the wrong direction. This interpolation strategy becomes specifically dangerous when the target language has morphological categories absent from the source vocabulary's dominant languages — for example, evidentiality markers in Quechua or vowel harmony suffixes in Turkish — because the "nearest neighbors" in the existing embedding space are phonologically similar but semantically orthogonal tokens, giving you confident-but-wrong initialization. The data condition that makes both strategies dangerous simultaneously is the intersection of very low fertility reduction (meaning the new tokens still appear rarely even after extension) and very small fine-tuning corpora (under ~10K sentences), because neither strategy has enough gradient signal to self-correct: Minixhofer et al. noted that WECHSEL's gains over random init largely disappeared below certain corpus size thresholds, suggesting initialization only matters when you have enough data to exploit a good starting point.

Given that the model's feedforward layers and attention heads were optimized for the original token distribution, vocabulary extension changes what the embedding layer sees but leaves all upstream weights frozen to old assumptions — how do you decide which layers to unfreeze during target-language adaptation, and what goes wrong if you get that decision wrong in either direction?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-223)
response:
The standard empirical finding, replicated across ULMFiT, mBERT probing studies, and the MAD-X adapter work, is that lower layers encode shallow morphophonological patterns while upper layers encode task-specific and semantic representations — which suggests a graduated unfreezing strategy: adapt lower layers first to reroute representations through the new token embeddings, then selectively unfreeze upper layers for task fine-tuning. But this heuristic breaks down for morphologically rich languages because the morphological processing that English distributes across syntax and semantics (handled in upper layers) is compressed into token-level surface forms in agglutinative languages, meaning the lower/upper layer division doesn't map cleanly onto the linguistic processing hierarchy you actually need to reorganize. Freezing too much — keeping all transformer layers fixed and only training the new embeddings plus a task head — produces the failure mode where the frozen attention patterns literally cannot route information from the new tokens effectively: the key and query projections were learned assuming the old token distribution, so the new embeddings occupy attention-space positions that receive low weight, and your new vocabulary tokens become representationally invisible even though they're grammatically present. Unfreezing too much with too little data produces catastrophic forgetting of the cross-lingual alignment that makes multilingual models useful in the first place — Üstün et al. (2022) on turking adapter configurations showed that full fine-tuning on small target-language corpora (under 15K sentences) could degrade zero-shot transfer to related languages by 15–30%, because the model overwrites shared representations rather than extending them. The practical resolution most supported by evidence is adapter-based adaptation (Houlsby, Pfeiffer variants) precisely because it sidesteps the unfreeze decision: adapters insert small trainable bottleneck modules while leaving pretrained weights frozen, meaning the original token-distribution assumptions are preserved in the base weights while the adapters learn to translate the new embedding positions into the existing representational scheme — MAD-X showed this consistently outperforms full fine-tuning in the low-resource regime across 41 languages on XTREME benchmarks.

Adapters preserve base weights but introduce their own bottleneck dimensionality as a hyperparameter — in the low-resource multilingual setting, what is the interaction between adapter rank, target-language fertility, and the risk of the adapter collapsing to a near-identity function that learns nothing?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-224)
response:
The adapter bottleneck rank determines how many independent directions in representation space the adapter can rotate or scale — a rank-64 adapter can express richer transformations than a rank-8, but in the low-resource setting the number of effective gradient updates you get is so small that high-rank adapters are underidentified: you have more parameters than the data can constrain, and the adapter converges to a near-identity because the path of least resistance for a randomly initialized bottleneck with insufficient supervision is to learn near-zero down-projection weights, producing outputs close to the residual stream passthrough. The interaction with fertility is direct and underappreciated: high fertility means each training sentence produces more tokens, which means more forward passes through the adapter per example, which sounds like more gradient signal — but those extra tokens are morphological fragments of the same word, carrying highly correlated gradients, so the effective sample diversity is lower than the raw token count suggests, and you get the worst of both worlds: apparent data volume that masks actual information sparsity. Pfeiffer et al.'s MAD-X experiments and subsequent ablations by Üstün suggest that for languages with fertility above ~4 tokens/word and training corpora under 10K sentences, adapter ranks in the 16–48 range consistently outperform both lower ranks (insufficient capacity to reroute representations from new embeddings) and higher ranks (underdetermined, collapses or overfits to surface token co-occurrences). The collapse failure mode is detectable but often missed: it shows up not as diverging loss but as frozen intermediate activations — the adapter output norm stays near zero throughout training while the task head compensates, meaning the model is effectively running without the adapter and you only discover this by instrumenting activation statistics rather than watching validation metrics. A compounding problem is that standard adapter initialization (near-zero for the down-projection, identity-ish for the up-projection) was designed to start as a near-passthrough and gradually activate — which is sensible for high-resource settings but is exactly the wrong inductive bias when you have few gradient steps, because the adapter may never accumulate enough signal to escape the near-identity basin before fine-tuning terminates.

response:
The most direct intervention is word-level gradient aggregation: instead of backpropagating a separate gradient signal for each subword token, you sum or average gradients across all tokens that derived from the same source word before the parameter update, effectively treating the word as the atomic unit of supervision and collapsing the correlated fragment signals into one. This is mechanically similar to what whole-word masking does during pretraining (used in RoBERTa and multilingual variants), and there's evidence it helps — Rust et al. (2021) in their tokenization analysis showed that models pretrained with whole-word masking had more coherent morphological representations for high-fertility languages, suggesting the gradient aggregation during pretraining was doing real work that per-token masking obscured. A more aggressive strategy is gradient projection via PCА or SVD on the adapter parameter gradients: you identify the low-rank subspace that the correlated fragment gradients actually span, project out redundant directions before updating, and concentrate the learning signal on the dimensions that carry novel information — this is related to techniques in continual learning (GEM, A-GEM) for preventing interference, but applied here to within-batch gradient redundancy rather than across-task forgetting. The dangerous interaction with multilingual alignment appears when you apply gradient manipulation globally rather than selectively to the adapter weights: if you're using a method like PCGrad (Yu et al., 2020) or gradient surgery to resolve conflicting gradients across languages in a mixed training batch, projecting away components that conflict with high-resource language gradients will systematically suppress the target-language signal, because by definition a low-resource language's gradient direction is underrepresented and looks like noise or interference from the perspective of the dominant languages. The subtler risk is with learning rate scaling strategies like per-parameter adaptive methods (Adam, Adafactor): because morphological fragment tokens for a low-resource language appear rarely in the training mix, their second-moment estimates are stale and their effective learning rates are inflated — which sounds helpful but actually means the adapter receives large, noisy updates on sparse tokens that overwhelm the careful low-variance signal you were trying to recover through aggregation, and Linzen (2020) and related work on tokenization artifacts suggests this is a systematic source of instability that standard adaptive optimizers were not designed to handle.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-226)
response:
Word boundary ambiguity propagates into gradient aggregation as miscollation error: if you incorrectly group subword tokens across what should be separate words (common in scriptio continua writing systems like Thai or classical Tibetan, or in agglutinative languages where clitics attach without whitespace), you're averaging gradients from semantically unrelated morphemes, injecting noise that is structurally indistinguishable from signal — worse than per-token gradients because you've added false correlation on top of the existing redundancy problem. For languages like Zulu or Swahili where the noun class prefix is orthographically fused to the stem and carries syntactic agreement information distributed across the clause, the "word" is simultaneously too large (it contains multiple morphosyntactic units that should receive differentiated supervision) and too small (its interpretation requires clause-level context), meaning the word boundary is the wrong aggregation unit regardless of whether you detect it correctly. Empirical evidence of this comes obliquely from Gerz et al. (2018) on the relationship between morphological complexity and NLP task performance, which found that languages with high paradigm size and fusion (as opposed to pure agglutination) showed steeper performance degradation on sequence labeling tasks — consistent with word-level aggregation destroying the within-word gradient distinctions the model needs. A concrete failure mode appears in Thai NLP: Thai lacks whitespace between words, so tokenizers either use a dictionary-based word segmenter (introducing segmentation errors that propagate directly into gradient groupings) or fall back to character or byte-pair boundaries (which may be more stable but abandon the linguistic motivation for aggregation entirely), and Limkonchotiwat et al. (2021) on WangchanBERTa showed that segmentation strategy choice had downstream effects on 4 out of 5 evaluated tasks, implying the boundary decision is load-bearing. The deeper theoretical problem is that the word is a language-specific and theory-dependent unit — in polysynthetic languages like Mohawk or West Greenlandic, a single orthographic word can encode what English expresses as a full clause, so aggregating gradients at the word level would collapse supervision across multiple predicate-argument relationships, and the right aggregation granularity is probably the morpheme — but unsupervised morpheme boundary detection for low-resource languages is itself an unsolved problem, creating a circularity where the quality of your gradient signal depends on linguistic analysis you don't have.

response:
The proposal is genuinely attractive and has partial precedent: attention entropy across subword tokens within a span does correlate with morpheme boundary probability in well-trained multilingual models — Kobayashi et al. (2020) and related probing work showed that attention heads in mBERT develop implicit sensitivity to morphological structure even without explicit supervision, with lower entropy (more focused attention) tending to align with morphologically coherent units. The mechanism you'd exploit is that when a sequence of subword tokens forms a coherent morpheme, the model's internal representations converge — hidden state similarity across those tokens is high, attention from outside the span treats them as a unit, and the gradient with respect to a masked prediction of one fragment is highly correlated with gradients for adjacent fragments — so a clustering or changepoint detection algorithm operating on hidden state trajectories could in principle segment the subword sequence into candidate morpheme spans without external annotation. The critical risk is confirmation bias amplification through self-referential supervision: if the model's current representations encode a wrong segmentation (which is likely early in training when the target-language embeddings are poorly initialized), using those representations to define gradient aggregation boundaries will reinforce the wrong groupings, making them more stable, which makes the representations more confidently wrong, in a loop that's hard to detect because task loss may continue to decrease as the model overfits to the internally-consistent but linguistically-incorrect segmentation. This is a specific instance of the broader bootstrapping instability problem studied in self-training literature — Yarowsky (1995) identified that self-training works when initial predictions are high-precision even if low-recall, but morpheme boundary detection from a poorly-initialized low-resource model violates that precondition because early hidden states for new vocabulary tokens are essentially interpolated noise, giving you low precision and low recall simultaneously as your supervision signal. A practical mitigation is delayed activation with a frozen reference model: run the first N training steps with per-token gradients to stabilize the new embeddings, then snapshot the model, use that snapshot's representations to infer aggregation boundaries, and continue training with those boundaries fixed — this breaks the real-time feedback loop at the cost of using a still-imperfect but at least stationary boundary detector, and is analogous to the target network trick in deep Q-learning (Mnih et al., 2015) where a frozen copy prevents the instability of chasing a moving target.
